speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext:
With respect to what has been said by the last two or three speakers, I am under the impression that the amendment moved by the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Pelletier) is not quite in order. I am not raising that point at the moment, but perhaps shall do so a little later. It brings up questions which are entirely new issues, and has nothing to do with the motion which has been placed before the house. In any event I am at a loss to understand just why this amendment is moved.
I have here extracts from Hansard which perhaps I had better read, indicating that in all quarters of this house there is an appreciation of the fact that there are campaign funds. Last year in the course of the discussion I myself said that there were campaign funds, and that they were necessary, and I discussed in this house- quite frankly the question whether or not the publicity of campaign funds would dry up their sources. There never was in mind any hiding of the fact that no political party can get along without some financial support. Mr. Bennett, at page 36 of Hansard of January 31, 1938 is reported as having said:
Contributions to political parties are not in any sense censurable.
And he went on at great length along the same line.
The right hon. leader of the government (Mr. Mackenzie King) as late as March 1, 1939, said:
Campaign funds are necessary for the purposes of an election. Is there anything w-rong with securing funds to help to propagate the principles in which one believes?
I have many other extracts from Hansard which tend to show that nobody denies the existence of campaign funds.
. My hon. friends of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation party also admit that there are campaign funds. They admit also that they require them. I have in my hand a clipping from the Vancouver Province, an advertisement entitled "The C.C.F. makes a frank appeal to you." In the advertisement there is a picture of my hon. friend the member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woods-worth). The appeal is made through Arnold Webster, First Vice-President, and it says:
I wish to address very briefly C.C.F. supporters throughout British Columbia-especially the thousands of sincere men and women who for one reason or another are not active members of our organization.
Many of you, at different times, have said something like this: "You know I can't safely associate myself with the C.C.F. My job makes that impossible, but I believe thoroughly in the cooperative idea; in fact, I'm with you and Mr. Woodsworth 100 per cent. If I can ever help the movement, let me know."
Mr. Webster apparently continues:
Well, I'm making that appeal to you now.
There will be a federal election this year. In every one of the sixteen constituencies in
B. C. the C.C.F. will have a good chance of victory if we are able to carry out the preliminary organizational work that is required.
You know, of course, that the old parties do not bother ordinary folk with such requests for money. Those who are making large fortunes out of the work and wealt h of others will gladly contribute thousands of dollars to the campaign funds of the Liberals and Conservatives-
I wish they would only bring them along, and I am sure the leader of the opposition would be glad to see some of them.
I should be very glad.

-and, as a result, control their policies and their decisions.
Against these privileged groups stands the
C.	C.F., the one important movement to-day that reflects the best in the hearts and minds of the common people of Canada.
We are beginning now to plan this year's campaign. Will you help us?
Money is needed to purchase radio time, to prepare attractive literature, to send organizers into neglected areas-to do the hundred and one things necessary to assure the success of C.C.F. candidates.

-a set amount per month and contributions will be privately acknowledged and remain confidential.

member of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation party was the hon. member addressing his remarks?

No. But I may in a
moment if my hon. friend wishes. I have in my hand Hansard of last year, containing the report of the debate on the address, in which the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell), who, I understand, is a prominent member of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation party, says:
The time has come, in the interests of clean and decent government in Canada, when political parties should be compelled to publish the sources of all their campaign funds.

I wish the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation in the house would be like the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation outside the house-
It is.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health

After all his rage, his anger, his indignation, at secret contributions, his party endorses and appeals for these same secret and confidential contributions.

If any one of us of the

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health

No.

Did my hon. friend say

carried on under government auspices for one political party or another, it still involves propaganda funds, and my hon. friends have no right to raise their hands in holy horror when other political parties are obliged to find means to carry on their work of education.

The reply of my hon. friend who was chairman of the committee last year is that that of itself would take ten years. Mr. Speaker, on a point of order-

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health

May I have an opportunity of saying one or two words before the amendment is ruled upon, if it is questioned. The minister was kind enough to refer to my rage and my horror regarding campaign funds. Let me say I do not think I exhibited any rage.

Chickens come home to roost.

May I refer to the advertised appeal by the first vice-president of our organization in British Columbia? We make those appeals publicly, through the press, and at every one of our meetings.

I understood that the minister sought to imply there was something sinister in the suggestion in the advertisement that contributions would be regarded as private and confidential. Oh, no.

It has happened. Moreover, I daresay they might be penalized in other ways. Having been treasurer of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation before the last general election, I am proud to be able to tell the house that we are quite willing to have our campaign funds thoroughly investigated, because although we won 400,000 votes, the only amount which was at my disposal as the national treasurer of the campaign fund was less than $2,000. It was less than $2,000 for the entire national campaign. We had hoped that we might put our leader on the air for at least one national broadcast, but were unable to do so. Consequently, when the inference is thrown at us that there is something sinister when we suggest that the relatively small contributions we received from our supporters ought to be kept private and confidential, I would tell the minister that really he is stretching the point.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: It is not sinister; it is only according to your principles.
The word used was " surreptitious," and that word has a sinister meaning.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: No. You condemned it yourself, and that is why I brought the matter to your attention-and for no other reason.

I would assure you, since our campaign funds and our method of collecting them has been brought before the house this afternoon, that at least we have never received hundreds of thousands of dollars from a power corporation.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
How do we know? How
does anybody know that?
As a matter of fact, I would ask the minister, who knows me very well, to accept my word for it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Of course I shall. But my hon. friend is not his whole party, any more than I am my whole party. And when one is willing to accept private contributions, that is where the danger arises.

I was treasurer before the last campaign, and we are quite willing to have an investigation. An investigation was held into some Liberal party funds, and the fact I have just mentioned was fully established at that time.
May I say I believe the suggestion made in the amendment is of interest to every hon. member, and to all parties. As the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Pelletier) indicated, from time to time newspaper articles appear and references are made in public speeches which tend to undermine confidence in the election of members to the House of Commons, and in the virtue of parliament. Consequently I believe the amendment is in the right direction. I therefore rise to do two things, first to set the minister right, if he thinks there w-as anything surreptitious-

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: "Surreptitious" only means hidden-go to your dictionary.

But certain words, by usage, acquire a particular connotation, and the minister knows that as well as I do.
As I said before, we are quite willing to have our funds fully investigated, if the other side is willing. I want to say only this, that we are supporting the principle of the amendment because we believe it is in the best interests of the house.
Question.

With reference to the
point of order raised by the Minister of Pensions and National Health (Mr. Power), I am of opinion that the amendment of the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Pelletier) is not in order, because the so-called amendment is not in fact an amendment at all. In order to support my decision I would refer the house to two similar decisions rendered on February 28, 1929, one by the Hon. Rodolphe Lemieux, the then Speaker of the House, and the other one by the then

speakeroldname: Hon. R. J. MANION (Leader of the Opposition) :
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to speak briefly to the resolution. The minister who introduced it, and some other hon. members who have spoken, have referred to the variation in the density of population as between constituencies. It seems to me in a country such as ours it is difficult to avoid that condition, and I doubt if there is any method whereby equality could be brought about.
At the same time some of the disparities shown are so great that they would appear to be unfair to one or other of the parties. However, one is confronted with the fact that some sections of our country, huge in area but sparse in population, must, in the interests of fair representation, have their representatives in parliament. I am not attempting to defend a system in which that condition exists, but I do believe that until those areas are more densely populated than they are at the present time, some of those inequalities must be accepted.
I do not believe that I would disagree with most of the minister's observations with respect to the general conduct of elections. It is my belief that conditions throughout the country are improving. I shall not go into detail in this connection, but I might point out by way of example that the son of a man who ran in one of the Quebec constituencies for election to the first parliament after confederation, and who had contested elections before confederation, told me that in those days the regular thing was to have the hogshead of whisky out in the back-yard, and to make it understood that the people who came round on certain days were free to use it, and that they expected it to be there. Such was the custom of that day, and I assume all candidates in certain sections of the country followed it. To-day that is largely done away
with, although there are times in certain elections when whisky is not in the hogsheads, but is passed round. In my own constituency I have never seen, on my side at any rate, anything in the way of the passing round of whisky. I think there is a good deal of exaggeration in the minds of many people throughout the country with respect to the powerful effects of the buying of the electorate.
I remember a very good story which actually happened in my constituency. One of the members who. preceded me-and a fine fellow he was, in his own way-at election times depended altogether upon the spending of money. He would go to the extent of mortgaging his house, and in every way putting up the last dollar he could raise. He carried on the election campaign in that way, and he did endeavour to buy votes when he could. On one occasion a friend of mine told me of a certain incident. He said that this old member-a good friend of mine, incidentally-asked him how such and such a village was going to vote. The reply was, "Well, there are about ninety votes there, and I fear they are all very doubtful." "How much money will it take to get them right?" The reply was, "About $5 each." The representative went out and bought every vote. But when the votes were counted they got only one of them.
I do not believe that there is any more use in attempting to buy votes to-day than there was in those days. I believe there is much exaggeration with regard to the matter. Certainly in my constituency, which the gentleman in question had represented in past years, I had no money to throw round. I paid what I thought were legitimate expenses, and carried on election campaigns as honestly as I could, during all the years I represented the constituency of Fort William-and I believe the situation is the same to-day. I have no doubt the hon. member who now represents that constituency is just as honest as I am. I found the seat could be won in a good and honest manner, and with no dishonest expenditures of money whatsoever.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
But it costs too much
just the same.

It does, I entirely agree,
and I also entirely agree that we should do all we can to do away with that extra cost. I agree also with the minister when he says that money is needed to run elections. He has given some evidence regarding our friends of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation. We have all heard that saying-I believe it was Sir John A. Macdonald's-that elections are not won by prayer.

Elections and Electoral Districts
It was Tarte.

Well, they were both
pretty good judges. In that book which my hon. friends opposite are so fond of quoting I discussed the whole question. My friend has missed a chance to look it up. I pointed out, and I point out again now, that there should be more publicity about campaign funds. There is nothing shameful about campaign funds, so long as they are honestly acquired.
And honestly used.

If people put up money
to help the party of their choice, because they believe in that party, and no strings are tied to that money, what is wrong? There is no more wrong in a man putting up $5,000 for the Liberal party or for our party than in someone putting up $5 for my friends to the left. The man who puts up the $5 may be hoping that his friends will get in so that he will get a job. The man who puts up $5,000 or $50,000 or $100,000 is just as honest as the man who puts up a small amount; he believes in the principles of the party he is supporting.

Suppose he gives to two
parties.

Well, he may have some
reason for doing so, and it is his money. Suppose he gives to the four parties, if you like. He knows that elections cost money. If he chooses to contribute to both Liberal and Conservative parties, and asks that no pledges be given or strings attached to that donation, there is nothing wrong with it that I can see, and I imagine I am just as honest as my hon. friends to my left, with all due respect to them. I believe we should bring this matter out into the open.
I hesitated about saying anything on this matter, because I think the minister dealt with the question very well, and the Speaker has now ruled the amendment out of order. But the other day I proposed to the Prime Minister that he bring the editor of the Ottawa Citizen before the bar of the house and make him prove some of his charges. I have here some of the charges he made, and I am going to road them, without comment. The hon. member who moved the amendment was trying to do what the editor of the Ottawa Citizen proposed. I have here half a dozen editorials from the Ottawa Citizen which made me see red. When I read these editorials, suggesting that both the old parties are a lot of crooks instead of decent citizens, it made me angry. Having been associated with political affairs in this house for twenty years, I 
say that members of parliament are just as honest as editors of newspapers or any other class, and I resent the suggestion that we in this house, whether Liberals or Conservatives or my hon. friends to my left, are a lot of crooks. I recall well an example of this irresponsible chatter; I was sitting in a smoking car-have I told this here before?
Yes.

Well, I heard a man criticizing both the old parties as a lot of crooks and I asked him on what authority he based his statement. He replied he did not base it on anything; he had just heard other people saying it, and he thought it the right thing to say. The irresponsible criticism of many people is of just the same type.
This is an example of what I object to. It is from the Ottawa Citizen of February 6:
National government is the next objective of amalgamated authority in Canada: it will include the economy of subscribing to the campaign funds of only one party.
That is not particularly bad. Here is another, of February 2:
It is the same old order, with no difference between parties excepting in the distribution of political patronage. Both parties are controlled by the same invisible government.
I say this party is not controlled by any invisible government or any individual, group or interest big or little. The government can answer for themselves, but I say that this party to-day is not controlled by anyone. We have campaign funds-I do not say we have much; I wish we had more. Obviously, we cannot have an organizer going round this country without someone paying him, and I cannot afford to pay him from my own purse. Our friends have contributed small amounts to carry on our organization, and I have nothing to be ashamed of. Not a dollar had a string on it in any shape, manner or form. The idea that there is anything wrong about doing that is ridiculous.
I should like to meet the men who give money away without any strings on it.

The hon. member apparently is of the type who does not think anyone can be honest.
This is another of these quotations from the Citizen; it is dated February 21:
The Conservative party will probably have to be satisfied with less than 40 per cent of the usual contributions as they are said to be distributed by the financial investors in the old game of party politics-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
"As they are said to be."

Elections and Electoral Districts

Exactly, that is the type of stuff.
In any casej there are signs that the Conservatives are becoming resigned to the prospect of being allowed a few cabinet seats in a national government as it is being demanded in the places where both parties collect the money to pay election expenses.
These are more of these ugly charges without any facts to substantiate them.
Another of January 28:
The power of the party machine to silence members-
This, I think, is a slander on every hon. member, including my hon. friends to my left.
The power of the party machine to silence members goes far beyond this influence of the central campaign fund. Members on the government side become involved in patronage deals. Members on the opposition side look forward to the day when they will again enjoy the spoils.
Another one, of which I have not the date,
states:
The whole democratic structure is threatened from within as well as from without. An independent parliament, free from dependence upon predatory campaign fund sources. . . .
I think this parliament is independent; I do not admit that this parliament is tied up to any campaign fund sources. Another statement is:
The party machines are largely financed by secret relations with contractors, promoters and privileged interests. Members become involved through indebtedness when election expenses are to be paid or later in the competition to display party loyalty before the next election-
The last I will quote is from the Ottawa Citizen of January 27:
Before the end of this session it will probably have been demonstrated to the paymasters of both parties-
I object to the statement that I have a paymaster. I repeat that I am under obligation to no individual, class, group, interest or anything else, neither is this party, and I object to the Ottawa Citizen making a statement like that. I resent such statements because they are slanders on all hon. members; as the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Pelletier) I think said, it is doing damage to and undermining democracy. I agree with that, and that is why I resent such statements. When I suggested that the editor of the Citizen be brought to the bar of the house, how did he defend himself? He demanded a judicial investigation. In other words, he accuses one of being a thief; the accused challenges him to give some proof, and the accuser says, " Oh, we will get a judge to investigate your whole life."

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No, he puts it up to you to prove you are not guilty.

Exactly, not the British system of assuming innocence until guilt is proved, but " you are guilty " first, and then he will send out a fishing expedition to see if he cannot find something against you. That is an irresponsible and improper method, and my hon. friends who move and support this amendment take the same attitude. So far as I am concerned I agree with the minister;
I do not consider that this fishing expedition would get anywhere. Men who contribute to [DOT] the campaign funds of both parties do so legitimately. I assume many who contribute may not want the fact known. Suppose a man is a manufacturer; he believes rather in the principles of the Liberal party, who claim they are low tariff people, although they do not always live up to it, but he is more in sympathy with the principles of the Liberal party than with ours. He may wish to contribute to the Liberal party funds, quite legitimately; he likes them and wishes to support them. But he may say, " If it is known that I have contributed to this fund and another party gets in, that other party might do something in the way of tariff changes which would hurt me." After all, he has a legitimate right to make his contribution in privacy, so I do not consider that an investigation would get anywhere at all.
It is almost six o'clock and I wish, before we take recess, to finish what I have to say. Many people contribute to party funds honestly. They believe in certain principles, and they wish to support the party that professes those principles. There are different kinds of dishonesty. Let me give an illustration of what I would call a worse piece of dishonesty than anything in regard to campaign funds. I was in Alberta not so long ago, travelling by automobile, and during the trip I heard over the radio a very prominent, if not the most prominent, social crediter in the province. He announced to his group-and apparently there was a large audience-that he was going to have a professor give expression that afternoon to the principles for which the capitalist system stood. That was done. The man who was master of ceremonies would make a clever and witty interjection every once in a while, more or less destroying the argument of the supposed professor of political economy who was setting out the principles of the capitalist system. Then, when the " professor" had finished, this other gentleman demolished the whole argument in a few well-chosen sentences. Of course it was a very bad argument, poorly put together, anyway; because the same man who made the interjections, the same man who demolished the argument, was the man who wrote both

Elections and Electoral Districts
sides of it. I found later that the supposed professor of political economy was the janitor of one of the provincial public buildings. Is that proper? Is that honest politics? I was driving with a prominent citizen of Calgary; I hung my head and said, " I am ashamed to think that any man in public life could descend to that type of campaign. No leader of either of the old parties would do that sort of thing." I say that type of campaign was much more discreditable than anything that has been done by either of the old parties.
I do not wish to argue against the Social Credit people. They have a perfect right to whatever attitude they choose to adopt, but at the same time 'I think we should all admit that we are honest. I do not think honesty is confined to any individual or any party in this house. In regard to my friends of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation party, during the election in London the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation candidate who opposed me made an appeal for funds, saying that if he were not helped financially he would not run. He put on a more elaborate and, so far as I know, more expensive campaign than I did; certainly he was on the radio a great deal more than I was. I have nothing to say against that; I find no fault with it at all, but let us agree that if you have not enough money yourself, you cannot carry on elections unless someone helps to pay the expenses. Whether a man contributes So ,000 or S5 to campaign funds, if there are no strings attached to it; if there is no crookedness in it; if the contribution is not made for the purpose of bringing about some dishonest act on the part of a party in power, then I say it is a perfectly legitimate contribution.
In closing, let me say that we want to cooperate with the minister, as I think all members of this parliament should cooperate, to lessen the cost of elections. They are far too expensive. It is unfair to the candidates of all parties. I think we should do everything we can to clean up election irregularities of all kinds in order that real public opinion may prevail and a fair deal given to all classes. In that way, by promoting public welfare, we may have a real democracy. So far as I am concerned, and speaking for my party, we will do everything we can in this committee, if it is appointed, to help clean up for the future. We are not worrying about the past. I do not believe in these fishing expeditions, and anyway, frankly 
I do not believe in charges of scandal. I never have believed in one party charging the other with doing something scandalous. Very seldom is anything proved of a scandalous nature. In the present unsettled condition of the world, unless a man is so certain of his facts that nothing can refute his charge I believe this sort of thing does nothing but undermine democracy, undermine our whole electoral system, undermine the freedom in which we all believe. I agree in large measure with what was said by the minister in introducing this resolution, and we will do all we can to help him clean up the elections of the future.

I wish to direct the attention of the Minister of Pensions and National Health (Mr. Power) to a problem which has arisen and which, I hope, will be taken into consideration by this special committee. I suggest to the minister that it would be advisable to broaden the terms of reference to the committee in order to enable consideration of a matter of vital consequence to many electors in British Columbia. In order to clarify the discussion I propose to move an amendment in terms which I hope he will accept. Briefly, I desire to direct his attention to a situation existing under the present provisions of the Dominion Elections Act, 1938, as it affects lumbermen, fishermen, miners and seamen. Under the act which was in effect during the federal general election of 1935, provision was made for what was called absentee voting, and special classifications were indicated therein for fishermen, including all those persons engaged in the fishing industry; lumbermen, including cruisers, loggers and so on; miners, including prospectors as well as workers in or about mines; and sailors, including all those engaged or employed on board ships or vessels. These persons were entitled to vote under special provisions contained in sections 99, 100, 101, 102 and so on, of the act. However, these provisions were abolished under the new act introduced at the last session. The chairman of the committee which sat last year, the hon. member for Swift Current (Mr. Both-

Elections and Electoral Districts
well), explained the situation to the hoyse, as reported on page 4246 of Hansard of June 24, 1938. At that time he said:
The committee found that the expense of absentee voting did not warrant our including it in this bill.
He goes on to say:
And it was by reason of the expense which was incurred in connection with absentee voting the committee decided that for the sake of a vote of that size we would not be warranted in inserting a clause which would deal with absentee voting.
He then enumerated other reasons why it was considered inadvisable to provide for absentee voting. I commend the minister when he endeavours to introduce amendments to the act to prevent any person from voting twice, but I had hoped that the new sections would not prevent certain classes of voters from voting at all. After a study of the act I have found that the workers engaged in the industries I have mentioned, that is lumbering. fishing, mining and those at sea, will not have an opportunity to exercise their franchise. We have done what it is possible to do in this country to encourage people to exercise their franchise, and it seems to me inadvisable that any obstacles should be placed in their way at this time.
I have made a study of the sections of the act in consultation with representatives of the organized workers in these various industries, and they confirm the conclusion which I stated last session, namely, that many of these workers will not have an opportunity of exercising their franchise. I hope that the committee will take into consideration ways and means of enabling those workers who must migrate from place to place in the pursuit of their vocations to exercise their voting rights on polling day. The act of 1938 not only abolished the provisions for absentee voting, but restricted to some degree the residential qualifications. Section 14, subsection 1, reads:
Save as hereinafter provided every person, man or woman, shall be qualified to vote and be entitled to be registered as an elector on the list of electors for the polling division in which he or she ordinarily resides-
The word "ordinarily" was introduced last session.
-at the time of the preparation and revision of the list of electors therefor.
It then goes on to give other qualifications. "Ordinary residence" is defined in section 16, subsection 2, as follows:
The place of ordinary residence of a person is, generally, that place which has always been, or which he has adopted as, the place of his habitation or home, whereto, when away therefrom, he intends to return. Specifically, when 71492-116
a person usually sleeps in one place and has his meals or is employed in another place, the place of his ordinary residence is where the person sleeps.
At the request of the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Neill) the bill was amended in some respects, and section 46 was amended by the deletion of the word "ordinarily" to make it possible for an elector within the electoral district in which he resides to present himself only at a rural poll to vote, provided he is vouched for by an elector already on the list in the poll. I submit that under the conditions which prevail in these industries in British Columbia a large number of men are actually disfranchised. When one considers the conditions of employment imposed on loggers, for instance, one must realize that the great majority of the camps at which these men work are outside the electoral districts in which they ordinarily have their residence. I confirmed this fact by inquiries since last session. The principal operations are on Vancouver island at Cowichan lake, Campbell river, and on the Queen Charlotte islands, these points being distant from the cities and towns where these men are recruited for these operations. Under the conditions prevailing in the industry they are unable to secure time off in order to vote, and they are unable to defray the expenses of returning to the polling division or the electoral district in which they have their ordinary residences.
The plight of the fishermen is still more serious. If polling day occurs when they are at the fishing grounds they are likely to find themselves in the predicament of being unable to return to their places of ordinary residence, which are usually in the vicinity of Vancouver. It might be possible to permit them to vote at the port from which they obtain their supplies when they are operating at the fishing grounds. There are many seamen employed on tugs and barges engaged in the coastwise trade who might be able to vote at a port of call but who certainly could not return to the polling division or the electoral district in which they are ordinarily resident.
The act of 1938 made provision for other classes of electors who are permitted to cast their votes outside the electoral district in which their names may have been placed on the list at the time of the issuance of the election writ. I refer to section 16, subsection 6, wherein provision is made for ministers, priests or ecclesiastics of any religious faith or denomination, for teachers and students. I submit that an attempt should be made to extend a similar privilege to the thousands of workers in the lumbering and



Elections and Electoral Districts
fishing industries and to those engaged at sea.
I do not wish to detain the house, but I do hope that my amendment will be acceptable to the minister. I am suggesting at this stage merely that the terms of reference to the committee should be broadened in order that the committee may take into consideration ways and means of dealing with this problem. I therefore move:
That the motion be amended by adding thereto the following clause:
(c) Methods whereby lumbermen, fishermen, seamen, and miners in the province of British Columbia may be enabled to exercise their franchise under the Dominion Elections Act, 1938.

Mr. Speaker, I must support the amendment moved by the hon. member for Vancouver North (Mr. MacNeil). There is no district in British Columbia outside my own where the necessities for some such plan are greater, and I do not except the district represented by the hon. member who has moved this amendment. Some of his electors may live in North Vancouver or Vancouver and go out to work in his riding, but if they live' in Vancouver or North Vancouver and go out to' work in my district, they are wholly disfranchised under the conditions which he has mentioned. As he said, the act which was passed a year or so ago made provision for voting in a polling station other than the one in which an elector was registered, but this was confined to the electoral district in which the man resided. That takes care of a number of cases in my district, but only to a limited extent.
There is no doubt that the present law does disfranchise a considerable number of the classes to which the hon. member has referred. This has been the case as far back as my memory goes, with the single exception of the election of 1935 when, as the hon, member has stated, there was inaugurated a system of what was called absentee voting, drafted in a large measure from the British Columbia system which works adequately in the smaller area of a province. But there were features about that system which did not make it so attractive as the hon. member suggests, and for this reason:	It was
founded on a system known as the fixed list, and the list was changed only once a year. In British Columbia we used to change the provincial list once every month; but in the dominion act passed here-and members will correct me if I am wrong-provision was made for a revision only once a year, with the result that in that province, where we have a good deal of a floating population, many more people were disfranchised than there

would be under the system now used. If they were there but if they did not get registered at these annual revisions, they were simply out of luck. I think the working men lost more votes under that method than under the system now proposed.
The hon. member for Vancouver North has pointed out that the act passed two years ago did make provision for school teachers and ministers of the gospel being allowed to vote if they moved into new territory, but it was upon the condition, which had to be definitely established, that they were going to become or had become permanent residents of the new district. A minister of the gospel, for example, had to prove that he was the ordained or accepted minister of his church, and a school teacher had to produce a certificate from the school board that he or she was legally and properly employed under contract for a certain period of time. The object of that was to do away with the danger, which must immediately suggest itself to the mind of anyone who considers these matters, that if you make it too easy for people to vote in a new district it is quite possible for a wealthy man or a wealthy party to bring in a couple of hundred men, say from a city district adjoining, keep them there for ten days-less than that would suffice-have them vote as temporary residents, and then return them. That is an even greater evil than the one my hon. friend is trying to avoid.
While he did not put it forward as his own opinion he referred to the argument of the high cost in the last election against having any more absentee voting. But I do not know whether the high cost was ever as definitely ascertained as it might have been, compared, for instance, with the cost of men voting at an advance poll. The cost there is quite comparable with that of an absentee vote.
Then he said that a great number of men who sought to vote were not allowed to vote. That happened in my district to the extent of several hundred people. They were thrown out against my protest simply because the deputy returning officers had not been thoroughly informed, or were incompetent, and they did not draw up the ballots in the way the act prescribed. They were given a certain number of blank ballots, and the act prescribed that if a man in the district of Comox-Alberni came to a deputy returning officer and said he wanted to vote in southeast Kootenay, the deputy returning officer must take a blank ballot, make a facsimile of the one used in southeast Kootenay, and

Elections and Electoral Districts
put down the name of every candidate, his occupation, residence and so forth. But in a great many instances the deputy returning officer was either ignorant or did not bother to do that. The very utmost he would often put down would be Jones, Brown and Smith, as the names of the candidates; he would not bother about their occupations at all, and many good votes-good in my opinion because the men were going to vote for me-were thrown out for that reason.
I know one case where the deputy returning officer, evidently in a spirit of good fellowship, apparently said to a man, "Whom do you want to vote for"? The man replied, "Jones"; the deputy returning officer wrote "Jones" down on the ballot and nothing else, and in that way perfectly good ballots were thrown out. That was on account of the system being new and the deputy returning officers not being sufficiently posted. Also they had to stop on a busy election day to make out a facsimile ballot. The case could have been met by furnishing the deputy returning officer with printed ballots for every riding in the province.
Even if the question of cost is considerable, there are other methods by which the proposal of my hon. friend, which I heartily endorse, could be carried out. His amendment, as I understand it, asks only that a method be considered whereby loggers, lumbermen, fishermen and so forth may be able to exercise their franchise.
In Australia, speaking from memory, I believe they have several systems of dealing with absentee voters. One of them is the post-card system. Nothing more stringent is required than for the voter to sign a postcard in the presence of the returning officer, and then under suitable restrictions and precautions it is mailed back to the place whence the voter came.
There is another method whereby they can vote absentees in person, something like that mentioned by my hon. friend. But the postcard method seems to work there without any opportunity of fraud and without any excessive cost, and I would hope that some system like that might be adopted. Surely we owe it to everyone that they should be allowed to exercise their franchise. And the fact that a voter's occupation takes him away at certain seasons of the year for two, three, six or eight months should not be allowed to stand in the way of his voting.
While I am speaking I might say a few words on the general proposals outlined by the hon. member who introduced this resolution. Some member speaking this afternoon

said that the subject matter as introduced last year was unpopular. But I submit it was not the subject matter that was unpopular; it was the bill that was universally unpopular. I regretted to hear the minister-perhaps I did not hear him arighb-speaking in a tone of laudation, I thought, of that misbegotten thing which was introduced last year.

speechtext: What was that?

The bill, the so-called purity bill. I thought he spoke this afternoon with some note of approval of it.
Mr. POWER Naturally.

It must have been owing to the fact that he is the putative father. There is an axiom in law in cases of disputed succession, that he is the father whom the marriage points out. I might paraphrase that by saying that he is the father who introduced the bill. The minister was associated with it in that regard, and in that regard only, in a very step-fatherly way. We all know that his ability and, above all, his sense of humour, would have entirely prevented him from having drafted of his own initiative such an abortion as the thing which was presented last year.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: Do not insult my child by saying that.

The bill was worse than the word I applied to it. I think it was a burlesque. Having read it a year ago, I have not now a clear recollection of all its provisions, but it certainly was a ridiculous and an unworkable thing. I wonder sometimes if it was not intended to be unworkable. One of the matters of interest to the group members was this thing called a corporation sole and two other positions at the same time, a sort of trinity proposition, and provision was made that the trinity had to be a lawyer or an accountant. It might well be that in ridings represented by social crediters there was no lawyer or accountant of their political party; they would be compelled to employ and be under the domination of this lawyer or accountant, who might be entirely opposed to their views, and he could make it very interesting and disconcerting in the conduct of the election. His powers are almost unbounded.
Something was said about limiting the costs to so much per head. Well, I am sorry, but if they put the costs at any reasonable figure I am afraid it will mean that I shall be unable to take part in an election. Ten cents a head, I assume, would be a reasonable cost.

Elections and Electoral Districts
and that would allow me a thousand dollars to spend on an election which ordinarily costs me between four and five thousand dollars. They say, "Oh, well, but it is done in Great Britain." But Britain is an established, settled country where a polling station, if it has eighty-five people to-day, will have eighty-six or eighty-four five or ten years from now. They know what it will cost. In our polling divisions we may have three hundred to-day and perhaps three at the next election, or perhaps four or five hundred. The conditions are so different that they cannot be compared, and I do not think any hon. member wants to be put in this position. You have struggled through the election with the difficulties of this corporation sole and these other capacities as well; you think you have won through at last, have kept within the margin you were told to keep in, that is that you must not spend more than ten cents a head, and have won the election.
I speak now not for myself, because it does not apply to me as I do not get party funds. But take the case of the man drawing party funds. He has been elected, or so he thinks; he has kept within the costs as far as he can honestly ascertain them; and six weeks after the election he gets a notice from Ottawa, "sorry, you have spent $4.81 more than you should have done, and you are unseated." He writes back and says, "No, I didn't; I kept well within the margin." "Oh, yes, but your proportion of the money spent by the headquarters of your party, your share, estimated to be so much, comes to so much, and therefore that puts you over the line." We do not want a machinery which will put members of parliament, no matter whether they are ourselves or some other candidate, in that position.
I agree heartily with what the minister said, that he thought the present bill, by merely being extended and expanded in certain regards, could do a great deal of what is aimed at in these resolutions. I heartily agree with him there. Take the case of the expenditures of sums of money. Under our present act the agent has to put in a return under oath of the amount of money he has received, how he has expended it and-note this-from whom he received it. Could one have anything more definite than that? But the way he gets out from under it under the present circumstances is this. He says, " I got $4,000 from Bill Jones and others." Bill Jones may have contributed $200 and the party fund or some corporation may have contributed the balance. That could be very easily adjusted by compelling the agent to state in the case

of every sum bigger than say $50, from whom he got it, and that would be done by a trivial change in the act which we have now.
We are told, and it is a sort of bait held out to us, that one of the results of this may be to reduce the costs of the candidates. Well, I cannot see it. I am afraid it is going to increase the cost to us, because we are going to be at the beck and call of the corporation sole fellow; in the middle of the election he may come forward and say, " You cannot hire that hall because you are exceeding your quota up to date," or something of that kind, and in this trinity of capacities he is likely to cost you a great deal of money. Above all that, there is the harassing anxiety when you are running an election-and it is an anxious enough time-that you will never know until it is all over, perhaps six weeks or perhaps six months afterwards, whether you have not been unseated through some trivial overexpenditure which you were perfectly incompetent or unable to stop at the time.
I know there are restrictions of this kind in Britain, but conditions there are totally different from what they are here, especially in the west where conditions change every month and every year. Now I would desire to see every one of the suggestions the minister has in his resolution put forward and carried to a conclusion. Certainly we want everything that is put there. But for the love of heaven and for the love of wretched candidates who will have to carry on, cut out last year's bill, or put it in the fire, or put it to some more ignoble purpose.

I should like to say one or two words in seconding the amendment to the resolution moved by the hon. member for Vancouver North (Mr. MacNeil). Before I do that I wish to congratulate the Minister of Pensions and National Health (Mr. Power) upon the subject-matter of the resolution which we discussed before recess. I am in the fullest accord with the two sections of that resolution, and I hope that not only will the committee be able to find ways and means of making a more satisfactory and possibly more just redistribution of seats than we have had hitherto, but that it will also find ways and means of keeping election expenses within reasonable bounds. I do not share the fears of the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Neill) that at some time I may over-spend, that I may spend more in my election than is allowed by the committee, because I am sure that I shall never have that much money to spend. Poverty has its advantages; I am free from that fear.

Elections and Electoral Districts
I wish it to be noted that the amendment moved by the hon. member for Vancouver North has reference to British Columbia only. The reason that absentee voting is so important to British Columbia is first, the economy of the country, which takes a great many of the voters away from their homes on election day; and second, because we have had for many, many years absentee voting in the provincial elections. I am not sure whether the first act was passed in 1920 or 1924, but I think it was the former year. I believe all federal members from British Columbia are agreed upon the value and the desirability of absentee voting. I never heard one of them oppose it. I remember that on one occasion shortly after the system had been put into effect there was some opposition because of irregularities which had developed, but that was overcome, and there has been no opposition since. I hope, therefore, hon. members will keep in mind that we are asking that this amendment apply only in British Columbia. Of course if hon. members from other provinces wish the same method to apply in their provinces, that is satisfactory to us.	.
I should like to read two sections from the revised statutes of British Columbia, chapter 84, having to do with provincial elections. Section 10S provides for absentee voting, and it will be observed, when I read the section, that in British Columbia absentee voting applies not only to persons outside their own electoral districts on election day but to persons who may be in their own electoral districts but not in the particular polling division in which they are registered. Section 108, subsection 1 of the provincial act reads:
For the purpose of exercising his franchise, any voter whose name is on the list of voters for one polling division of an electoral district, and who is absent from that polling division on the day on which the poll is held, may obtain an absent voter's ballot-paper in any other polling division of the same electoral district and may record his vote in the manner provided in this section.
That section covers all of British Columbia, with the exception of the electoral districts in the cities of Vancouver, Victoria and New Westminster.
Section 109 is still wider than section 108. Subsection 1 of section 109 provides:
For the purpose of exercising his franchise at any general election, any voter whose name is on the list of voters for one electoral district, and who is absent from that district on the day on which a poll is held therein, may obtain an absent voter's ballot-paper for that district in any polling division of any other electoral district in which a poll is being held, and may record his vote in the manner provided in this section.
As I said before, in British Columbia we have had this method of voting for the past twenty years. The people have become accustomed to it. Loggers and others who, on election day, are away from their homes, or from the places where their names appear bn the voters' lists, feel that they have something to do with the election of the government when they are allowed to exercise their franchise.
It seems to me that democracy means the extending to every class within the country the privilege of taking part in the government of the country. To the extent that we can do that, and to the extent that all classes can take part in the government of the country, jujt to that extent do we have democracy. And to the extent that any class, or section of any class, is restricted from taking part in the government of the country, or in electing its representatives, to that extent is our democracy limited.
A great deal of argument has been made about the cost. In my opinion in the election of 1935 the high cost was on account of the inexperience of the election workers. I am sure that with better organization and the freer use of the absentee method of voting the cost would be much less. In the amendment we are asking to have this method applied to four different occupations, namely, lumbermen, fishermen, seamen and miners. I would point out to the house that in the provincial elections in British Columbia absentee voting is not restricted to any particular occupations. As I have indicated in the two sections I have read, any person who is not in his polling division or electoral district on election day may vote by absentee ballot. I would ask the government to give the most favourable consideration to the amendment to enlarge the scope of the reference to the committee, before deciding to turn the amendment down.

Mr. Speaker, with respect to the amendment moved by the hon. member for Vancouver North (Mr. MacNeil), I can only say that last year in committee considerable time was spent in discussing the subject of absentee voting. If the amendment is in order, which I doubt very much, my first objection to it would be that it applies only to British Columbia. If the act is going to be amended to provide for absentee voting, then it would appear to me that there should be general application so that it would apply to every province. The maritime provinces must be in exactly the same position as British Columbia, and the same observation would apply to those constituencies facing on the

Elections and Electoral Districts
great lakes. The sailors on those lakes will be absent from home, just in the same way as the seamen, lumbermen and fishermen of British Columbia may be absent.
The hon. member has referred to my remarks of last year as reported at page 4246 of Hansard. On that occasion I said:
The committee found that the expense of absentee voting did not warrant our including it in this bill. For instance, in the election of 1935 there were 5,334 votes polled under the absentee voting provision. We found that 1,533 of them were rejected. The cost of absentee voting was approximately $250,000, or $65 plus, per vote. And it was by reason of the expense which was incurred in connection with absentee voting the committee decided that for the sake of a vote of that size we would not be warranted in inserting a clause which would deal with absentee voting.
If expense is no object, then I assume we can provide for every person in Canada, no matter where he or she may be, exercising his or her franchise on election day. Certainly machinery can be set up in some way whereby every man would have an opportunity to vote, either before or after the election, and whether or not he was in his own constituency or polling subdivision.
However, I believe the committee had before them all the representations which have been made this evening, and they gave every consideration to the matter. Their conclusion was that they were not justified in inserting the absentee provisions which were in the 1934 act.
Was any other method of dealing with the problem considered by the committee?

Various methods were discussed. As a matter of fact, representations were made to the committee by an organization of sailors on the great lakes. Representations were made with respect to the exercising of their franchise, and I believe a resolution of two or three pages was presented in which suggestions were made which would have had the effect of permitting them to vote. However, so far as I am concerned as a member of the committee-and I assume other members will have the same view-I am ready to reconsider the matter, if it is deemed advisable. But I do not see how the same committee can reach a conclusion different from the one they arrived at last year. If the amendment is in order I would consider discussing the matter again-although I see the hon. member for Leeds (Mr. Stewart) shaking his head. I assume he is of the same opinion I am, namely that it will not get any further than it did last year.

I had
no intention of speaking on this motion, but in view of certain statements that have been made during the debate I should like to make a few brief remarks. It has been suggested that the social credit proposals were used as a bribe during the last provincial election in Alberta. Hon. members making those charges show complete ignorance of the growth of the social credit movement in that province. That movement started at least three years before the election. It was started as an economic movement, with no intention at that time of political action. An attempt was made to persuade the United Farmers of Alberta government to introduce legislation implementing the social credit proposals, and it was not until that government had definitely refused to take any action in that regard that finally the people of Alberta from one end to the other demanded of Mr. Aberhart that he organize politically. In view of that it cannot possibly be maintained that social credit was used as a bribe, because the people cannot very well bribe themselves, and it was as a result of the demands of the people that the action was taken.
I will, however, agree that in the last election social credit was used as a bribe, not by the Social Credit party but by the leader of the Liberal party in Alberta.
Oh, oh.

I hear one hon. gentleman
laugh.	I quote this statement from the
Edmonton Journal of August 17, 1935:
Many Liberal candidates and speakers are denouncing social credit with great vigour. But no matter how completely one may agree with what they have to say on the subject, it is impossible to forget the stand that their leader has taken and the pledge that was given in the party's platform. A statement from Mr. Howson was published in the editorial column of the Medicine Hat News on January 14 last, which read:

You may be surprised to learn that the Liberal party was in the field on behalf of social credit before the Alberta movement started. . . . Mr. Aberhart has promised his followers no more than the Liberal party has. As a matter of fact he has promised them less.

There was no hint of
humour about it the day I heard it.

people who can contribute these large sums are large financial corporations, and they are willing to contribute as long as the present reactionary policies are maintained. That is what the people object to; they object to

large financial corporations being able to support a reactionary government. That I think is a fair statement. speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext:
I suggest that the amendment moved by the hon. member for Vancouver North (Mr. MacNeil) is out of order on two counts. The first is that the statement made in it is absolutely inaccurate. The amendment is that the motion be amended by adding the following clause-to study, I assume:
(c) methods whereby lumbermen, fishermen, seamen and miners in the province of British Columbia may be enabled to exercise their franchise under the Dominion Elections Act, 1938.
But they are able now to exercise their franchise, excepting only a certain few who happen to be away from their homes. Of all the people of Canada, those who took advantage of the absentee voters clause during the last election numbered only 5.000. Of all the people in Canada who could take advantage of the absentee voters clause, only 5,000 did so.
That does not make the amendment out of order.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext:
It is out of order, because an inaccurate statement is made. The amendment says that lumbermen, fishermen, seamen and miners should be enabled to exercise their franchise. If it had said "in order that certain miners who are absent from their homes may be able to exercise their franchise," I would be able to understand it, but it makes the gratuitous statement that somebody is endeavouring to prevent lumbermen, miners, fishermen and seamen from exercising their franchise.
Apart from that, Mr. Speaker, I should like to draw your attention to the fact that this amendment raises a new issue. The resolution before us deals with redistribution and with political expenditures. What is sought to be referred to the committee here is an amendment to the elections act, which act was thoroughly discussed by the committee for three years and passed by this house last year. I do not think it is the opinion of the house that the reference should be enlarged, and in any event no proper notice was given which would permit raising the issue.

I think the minister is
stretching a point when he says I offered a gratuitous, inaccurate statement. In my remarks I endeavoured to outline the problem, and I would direct your honour's attention to the fact that a ruling was given previously this session, when the act to amend the Fisheries Act was under consideration, to the effect that when the general act was under review it was in order for an hon. member to bring in an amendment.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: But no part of the Dominion Elections Act is under consideration at the moment.

I am coming to that. In his remarks the minister stated that he might take into consideration certain amendments to the Dominion Elections Act which would strengthen its provisions in dealing with political expenditures; and in that regard he did suggest that the Dominion Elections Act would be under review again by this committee, in some respects at least.
I hope the minister does not press the point of order. I see no objection to having the committee give consideration to this vital problem. I have not suggested any particular solution; I have merely asked that the committee review the problem in the light of additional evidence now available.

There is only one point at
issue, namely, whether a member of this house has the right to add something to a reference to a committee. I do not think it has ever been contended that a member has not the right to move an amendment to extend the terms of reference, and that is all that is being sought in this case. The minister himself has presented a resolution referring two matters to the committee; another member of the house rises and asks that the terms of reference be extended in the present instance by including fishermen, lumbermen, miners and seamen in British Columbia.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health

While my hon. friend has had experience in the Department of Trade and Commerce, perhaps he has not appreciated, as I believe many hon. members have, the great place which the film has made for itself in ordinary business and in various activities throughout the world. Probably he does not realize that other countries are adopting this medium for the promotion and spreading of intelligence, information and, if you like, entertainment for the working out of certain national interests.
That is the purpose of what we are* doing. When the hon. member speaks of the term "commissioner" as being a glorified name to impress other departments-well, I think that is hardly worthy of him. That is not the purpose at all. As a matter of fact, it does not matter particularly to me whether the man in charge is called a commissioner or by some other name. I regarded that as a suitable name to describe his functions.
I think my hon. friend does not show a complete appreciation of what we want to do. It is this, that the director of the bureau and may I say that I can join with him in paying tribute to the efficiency of the director-has enough to do in running the bureau and in dealing with the production of films.
The commissioner will have entirely different work to do. Under the board itself, which will frame policies and which will decide as to national films, if you like, and as to the work which is to be carried on, the commissioner will himself have a sphere in which he may work, and will do work which in my opinion the director of the bureau will not be able to do. There will be sufficient scope for work for both of them.
Had I the time I might dwell upon what I mean by the production of national films. I said the other evening there might be a need or a desirability for the production of a national film which would appeal to the whole country, and which could not be produced by any one department. As we have it now, we have half a dozen departments of government which produce films, but which deal only with the particular work of their own department. But that does not touch what we mean by a national film.
Perhaps from some notes I have before me I might give a somewhat more complete description of what is meant by a national film.
I have spoken of what is meant by a departmental film, namely one which would serve the needs of any one department. For instance, the Department of Trade and Commerce might require a film in connection with the promotion of the sale of goods. One [Mr. Stevens.1
might be required by the Department of Transport, which would deal with encouraging tourist traffic. Then, we might require another for the Department of Labour, and still another for the Department of Mines and Resources, which might deal particularly with the mining of gold or any other mineral. Then we might have a film which would appeal to the whole country; sometimes they are known as prestige-building films. Usually in a dramatic or imaginative way they show different aspects of a country's life. They show its work, its resources, and its achievements in the various fields of social and industrial endeavour. Such films are designed to sell the idea of a country in terms of national perspective, so as to build up an increased interest and a favourable sentiment towards a nation and its people, at home and abroad.
The other evening the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Green) offered the suggestion that provision be made for the distribution of national films designed to help Canadians in all parts of Canada to understand the ways of living and problems of Canadian people. That conveys pretty well the idea of what is meant by a national film.
I am not going into the matter at greater length, but I would say that if the committee believes there is work to be done by way of having national films which appeal to the country at large, entirely distinct from the work of any one department, then I think we have room for the formation of a film board, to be headed by a film commissioner, which would carry out that work entirely in addition to the work of coordination of the operations of the various departments, to which I made reference before.

subtopic: REVIEW OF GOVERNMENT FILM ACTIVITIES- INTERDEPARTMENTAL COMMITTEE TO CENTRALIZE DISTRIBUTION
speechtext:
Yes. The moving picture bureau under Mr. Badgley of the Department of Trade and Commerce, is a branch for which I have a good deal of respect. While I was never Minister of Trade and Commerce I was acting minister of that department occasionally when the then minister, the hon. member for Kootenay East (Mr. Stevens) was away. Thus I became acquainted with the work of Mr. Badgley and his group, and I have a great deal of respect for him.
In view of the comparatively small amounts that are being spent by the other departments mentioned by the minister, who said the mines branch was spending some 820,000 while various others were spending less, some as little as $5,000, is it not sufficient to leave things as they are and allow Mr. Badgley to carry on exactly as he is doing, with this modification: If other departments want moving picture work done, it should be done by Mr. Badgley's branch? If it is necessary, from the point of view of other departments, to have some check on Mr. Badgley, that might be effected by some kind of interdepartmental committee. Take the mines branch, as a good illustration. Possibly there will be more and more work done on behalf of that branch, which has to do with one of our great industries. The Department of Agriculture might be another branch that would have a good deal of work to be done. If Mr. Badgley had something in the way of an interdepartmental committee to assist him, he could do exactly what would be done by the new commission proposed by the minister.

We have Mr. Badgley, an able civil servant, who has been doing splendid work: the minister himself said so, and I know that to be the case from what little experience I have had with that bureau. He is not to be encouraged to carry on his work on the wider scale which the minister believes will be necessary. Instead of that, and instead of attaching greater importance to his position, the government is thinking of bringing in some outsider, no doubt a man who has had something to do with moving pictures, putting him over Mr. Badgley and forming a new bureaucratic branch of government. I say this sincerely, and with no thought of merely opposing the minister: I believe we have enough departments of government now.
I remember many years ago in this house listening to a speech by the Minister of Mines and Resources (Mr. Crerar); as I remember it, he was then in opposition. I have never forgotten that speech; it is the only one he ever made that I remembered- he is behind the curtain there, so I will tell him this. In his speech he showed the rapid increase in the number of civil servants, year after year. I do not wish to steal the thunder of my hon. friend the member for Kootenay East (Mr. Stevens), but as he pointed out the other day, every time a new branch of any kind is established it starts out with an officer and a secretary. Within a few months the secretary has a secretary, and of course there is always a messenger in the beginning as well. Then, before you know it, you have a real branch of some department built up, and the more employees they get the more important they think they are. It is a strange thing, but I am informed by outstanding civil servants that many of them at any rate, if not all, judge their importance by the number of employees they have under them. So it seems to be a habit, whenever a new branch is established, to build it up and make it important. I could give many instances which I remember. I have one in mind in particular, but I do not wish to name it because I believe it performs a useful service. I can think of others, however, that have started in the same way and have been continually built up. Finally, instead of spending the $125,000 which is indicated for this year, we shall be spending perhaps S250.000, and we shall have another bureaucracy taking over part of our government.
I say to the minister in all sincerity that he should hold up this bill a little longer, give it further consideration and see if a scheme cannot be worked out, as I feel sure it can, whereby Mr. Badgley may remain in

National Film Board
control of his own bureau, assisted by something in the way of an interdepartmental committee made up of representatives of the other departments interested. These might include the Department of Mines and Resources and perhaps the Department of Agriculture. The minister of that department, being such a good friend of the Minister of Trade and Commerce, probably would be of particular assistance. That is an aside, however; that is not really of any great importance.
